contributions.headingText: Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) is an inborn or acquired error of immunity characterized by lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, and an increased risk of lymphoma. It is associated with germline or somatic defects in the FAS-mediated apoptosis pathway and the accumulation of αβ CD4/CD8 double-negative T (DNT) cells.
4A01.22 Immune dysregulation syndromes presenting primarily with lymphoproliferation

ALPS with germline FAS mutation (ALPS-FAS), either homozygous (autosomal recessive) or heterozygous (autosomal dominant); ALPS with somatic FAS mutation (ALPS-sFAS); ALPS with other specified FAS-pathway germline mutation (FASLG, CASP10, CASP8, FADD); ALPS with unknown underlying mutation (ALPS-U) {20538792; 31953710}
The lymph nodes and spleen are the main sites of involvement; less commonly, extranodal sites {28395106}, including the bone marrow {27846610}, are involved.

Clinical features include lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, an increased risk of lymphoma, and a high risk of sepsis after splenectomy {9028957; 11418480; 21885602; 24398331}. ALPS-FAS is usually diagnosed in early childhood, whereas ALPS-sFAS is diagnosed across a broad age range {20360470; 15459302}. Coexisting IgG4-related disease may occur {28478106}.

Radiological features

The PET imaging features of ALPS overlap with those of lymphoma {31689275}.

The global prevalence of ALPS is unknown; a recent systematic review relied on data predominantly from the USA, Italy, and France {33963613}. FAS mutations accounted for 85% of cases of ALPS; 87% of these mutations were germline.
Genetic factors are characterized by germline or somatic mutations in FAS or genes encoding the FAS pathway {20538792}.

FAS pathway gene mutations lead to a failure of lymphocyte apoptosis {9028957; 7540117} and increased proliferation {17724145; 27099149}, resulting in the persistence of physiological CD38+, CD45RA+, IL-10+ CD4+, CD8+, and DNT cell populations {33170215}. Failure of FAS-dependent T-cell immune surveillance {24487434} and FAS-deficient germinal-centre B cells {33237303} may contribute to the predisposition to lymphoma.
The lymph nodes and spleen are enlarged and homogeneous in appearance. Firm, fleshy, or necrotic areas should be sampled to exclude lymphoma.

Lymph nodes are enlarged by reactive follicular hyperplasia and pronounced pale-staining paracortical hyperplasia, with admixed proliferations of DNT cells and polytypic plasma cells. Progressive transformation of germinal centres, Castleman disease–like histology, or superimposed plasmacytosis {9811346} may mask histological findings {34474549}. Rosai–Dorfman disease is found in about a quarter of ALPS lymph nodes {24398331; 15958855}. Similar infiltrates occur at extranodal sites, including the spleen and bone marrow {28395106; 27846610; 9811346}.

Immunohistochemistry

The DNT cell population is positive for CD45RA, negative for CD45RO, and positive for cytotoxic markers, including perforin, TIA1, and CD57 (see #29848Box 5.03) {9811346; 12657942; 29296752}.

Differential diagnosis

The differential diagnosis includes RAS-associated leukoproliferative disease; unicentric Castleman disease (UCD), especially the mixed/plasmacytic subtype, and idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD); IgG4-related disease; Rosai–Dorfman disease; and lymphoma. Although IgG4-related disease and Rosai–Dorfman disease can co-occur with ALPS, the diagnosis of KSHV/HHV8-negative multicentric Castleman disease is definitionally excluded in the setting of ALPS {28087540}. ALPS may mimic T-cell lymphoma by its high proliferation index, unusual immunophenotype, and extranodal involvement (including the bone marrow) {34492736}.

Bone marrow involvement by benign lymphoproliferation must not be overinterpreted as lymphoma {27846610}.

Numerous ALPS-like primary immune regulation disorders share an autoimmune lymphoproliferative phenotype (see #29847Table 5.02).

Germline and acquired mutations should be assessed according to diagnostic guidelines {20538792; 33356695; 33995372; 26323380}. Similar FAS death domain mutations are also found in lymphoma {29481902}. ALPS DNT cells have a restricted TCRVβ repertoire {18566410}, raising the concern for possible false positive T-cell clonality results.

Essential: > 6 months of benign, non-infectious adenopathy and/or splenomegaly, peripheral blood flow cytometry showing normal or increased lymphocyte count; αβ DNT cells > 1.5% of total or > 2.5% of CD3+ lymphocytes; detection of FAS, FASLG, CASP8, FADD, or CASP10 mutation.

Desirable: a probable diagnosis can be made if typical lymph node findings are also present – however, expanded lymph node αβ DNT cells do not substitute for peripheral blood flow; elevated plasma vitamin B12, serum FASL, and IL-10; autoimmune cytopenias with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia; a compatible family history can support a probable ALPS diagnosis.

ALPS is associated with an increased risk of B-cell lymphomas, including classic Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, and (rarely) T-cell lymphoma and histiocytic sarcoma {11418480; 21885602; 24398331; 20216376}.
